title: Preventing emergencies & spotting the unwell patient
blurb: Medical histories, recognising risk, team training and rehearsed roles: how a practice stops emergencies happening and catches them early.
question: A patient with type 1 diabetes arrives for a long morning appointment. While you seat them, they mention they skipped breakfast because they were running late, and you notice their medical history was last updated two years ago. What should you do before treatment starts?

teach.h: The best emergency is the one that never happens
teach.body: Many medical emergencies in dental practice happen to patients with a condition the team could have known about: diabetes, asthma, angina, epilepsy, allergies, or simply a lot of anxiety. Prevention means three things. Know your patient through an up-to-date medical history. Reduce the risk on the day. Make sure the whole team is trained, rehearsed and knows exactly where the kit is, so that if something does happen, the response is fast and calm.

teach.caption: Each step feeds the next. A scenario practice that exposes a gap (say, nobody knew where the oxygen key was) changes how you prepare next time.

teach.h: The medical history is your early warning system
teach.body: A full written medical history is taken at the first visit and updated regularly, usually at each new course of treatment. It is signed, dated and reviewed by the dentist. At every appointment someone should also ask: "Has anything changed with your health or medicines since we last saw you?" Record the answer in the notes at the time. A history that is two years old may miss a new heart condition, a new blood thinner or a new allergy.

teach.text: Training is not a certificate you collect once. A team that has never rehearsed together loses vital minutes, and not knowing where the emergency kit is counts as one of the most serious failings in a practice.

items: Written history updated regularly (each new course of treatment); verbal check at every visit.
Use the history to spot risk and prepare: eaten? inhaler? GTN? allergy flagged?
Stop and alert the dentist at early warning signs; assess with ABCDE.
One leader allocates roles: CPR, caller, runner, recorder, reception.
Train regularly (GDC recommends 10 h per cycle, 2 h a year) and rehearse scenarios as a team.

summary: You can now explain how a practice prevents medical emergencies: keeping medical histories current, spotting at-risk patients and preparing for them, recognising early warning signs, and making sure a trained team rehearses scenarios and knows its roles and where the kit is kept.

A.q: A regular patient attends for a filling. Their full medical history was completed at their check-up last month. What should happen at today's appointment?
options: Nothing, as the history is still recent
A full new written history is required
Ask if anything has changed and record it
Only check the history if they look unwell
A.why: The history should be confirmed at every appointment by asking about changes to health or medicines, and the answer recorded at the time.

whyNot.0: Health can change within weeks, for example a new medicine, so it must still be checked verbally.
whyNot.1: A full rewrite isn't needed every visit; a verbal check with a record is the expected step between full updates.
whyNot.3: Many risks (a new allergy, a new blood thinner) give no visible sign, so you can't rely on how the patient looks.

A.q: A patient with asthma is booked for a scale and polish. Which step best reduces the risk of an asthma attack during treatment?
options: Asking them to bring their inhaler
Giving salbutamol from the kit first
Booking them only for the afternoon
Treating them sitting bolt upright
A.why: Asking asthmatic patients to bring their own reliever inhaler, and keeping it to hand, means it can be used at the first sign of symptoms.

whyNot.1: Emergency drugs are for treating an emergency, not for routine pre-treatment of every asthmatic patient.
whyNot.2: Appointment time isn't the key factor for asthma; having the reliever to hand is.
whyNot.3: Posture may help comfort, but it doesn't replace having the inhaler ready.

A.q: A patient collapses in the waiting room and four staff arrive at once. What should happen first to make the response effective?
options: Everyone starts CPR together
Each person decides their own task
The most junior person phones 999
One leader allocates clear roles
A.why: A single leader allocating roles prevents duplication and makes sure every task (999, kit, CPR, recording) is covered.

whyNot.0: Only one person can do compressions at a time; others are needed for the call, the kit and the AED.
whyNot.1: Without a leader, tasks get duplicated or missed, which wastes time.
whyNot.2: Seniority doesn't decide who calls; the leader allocates the caller as part of the plan.

B.q: A very anxious patient tells you they have fainted at the dentist before. Which measure is most likely to prevent a faint today?
options: Treating them sitting fully upright
Treating them lying flat in the chair
Asking them to skip breakfast that day
Giving them oxygen before starting
B.why: Fainting is caused by a temporary fall in blood flow to the brain; treating the patient lying flat helps keep blood flowing to the brain.

whyNot.0: Sitting upright makes a faint more likely, because blood pools away from the brain.
whyNot.2: Missing meals makes fainting more likely, not less.
whyNot.3: Oxygen isn't given routinely to prevent fainting; position and reassurance are the key measures.

B.q: Midway through treatment, a patient with diabetes becomes pale, sweaty and muddled in their answers. What should you do first?
options: Carry on so the treatment is finished
Wait to see if it passes in ten minutes
Stop and alert the dentist straight away
Phone their GP surgery for their advice
B.why: Pale, sweaty skin and confusion in a diabetic patient are warning signs (possibly hypoglycaemia). Stop, alert the dentist and assess the patient.

whyNot.0: Carrying on ignores warning signs that can quickly become a collapse.
whyNot.1: Waiting lets the condition worsen; early action is the whole point of spotting warning signs.
whyNot.3: The team must act now in the practice; the GP isn't the right first call in an emergency.

B.q: How much medical emergencies CPD does the GDC recommend a dental nurse completes?
options: 5 hours per cycle, at least 1 a year
10 hours per cycle, at least 2 a year
15 hours per cycle, at least 3 a year
2 hours per cycle in total, any year
B.why: The GDC recommends at least 10 hours of medical emergencies CPD per five-year cycle, with at least 2 hours every year.

whyNot.0: Five hours per cycle is the recommendation for decontamination and for radiography, not medical emergencies.
whyNot.2: This overstates the recommendation; it is 10 hours per cycle.
whyNot.3: Two hours is the minimum each year, not the total for the whole cycle.

C.q: Why should the whole team regularly run simulated medical emergency scenarios in the practice?
options: To find gaps before a real emergency
Because it replaces checking the kit
So only the dentist needs any training
To avoid having to call an ambulance
C.why: Rehearsal shows up delays and gaps (unclear roles, kit hard to reach) so they can be fixed before a real patient needs help.

whyNot.1: Scenarios don't replace kit checks; RCUK still expects at least weekly checks by named people.
whyNot.2: Every team member needs training to their role; emergencies can happen when the dentist is busy or absent.
whyNot.3: Practice improves the team's response; a serious emergency still needs a 999 call.

C.q: A patient's history shows they have angina. What should you ask them to do for their appointments?
options: Take an aspirin before every visit
Bring their own GTN spray with them
Avoid eating for two hours before
Come only when a doctor is present
C.why: Patients with angina should bring their GTN spray so it is to hand if chest pain starts.

whyNot.0: Aspirin isn't taken routinely before treatment; in the kit it's for a suspected heart attack.
whyNot.2: Fasting has no role in angina and may make the patient feel unwell.
whyNot.3: Dental teams are trained to manage emergencies; a doctor doesn't need to be present.

C.q: On a dental nurse's first day at a new practice, why must they find out where the emergency kit is kept?
options: It is only needed for the annual audit
Emergencies can happen on any day
The kit is moved to a new place weekly
Only new staff are allowed to fetch it
C.why: An emergency can happen on day one; RCUK expects all staff to know where all resuscitation equipment is kept in their area.

whyNot.0: Knowing the location matters for patient safety every day, not just for audits.
whyNot.2: The kit should be kept in a fixed, known place so it can be found fast.
whyNot.3: Any member of the team may need to fetch it; the leader allocates the runner.

reteach.title: Think like a pilot before take-off
reteach.question: Pilots run checks before every flight and practise emergencies in simulators. How does a dental team do the same thing?

blocks.body: A pilot never skips the pre-flight checklist, even on a route they've flown a hundred times. Your checklist is the medical history: "Anything changed? New medicines? Eaten today? Got your inhaler?" Pilots also train in simulators so their hands know what to do when an alarm sounds. Your simulator is the scenario practice: same room, same kit, same roles, so a real emergency feels familiar rather than frightening.

items.label: Flag conditions
items.sub: Diabetic? Book so they can eat normally first

items.label: Check the history
items.sub: Anything changed? Eaten? Inhaler or GTN with them?

items.label: Watch the patient
items.sub: Colour, breathing, behaviour; speak up early

items.label: Record and review
items.sub: Note any concerns for next time

blocks.text: Prevention is a team habit, not one person's job. The receptionist who notices a patient looks grey in the waiting room is preventing an emergency just as much as the nurse in the surgery.

explain.body: A written history is taken at the first visit and updated regularly, typically at each new course of treatment, then signed, dated and reviewed by the dentist. At every visit, ask whether anything has changed and record the answer straight away.

steps.label: Written history
steps.sub: First visit and each new course

steps.label: Record it
steps.sub: In the notes, at the time

test.q: Which best describes good practice for medical histories?
options: Taken once when the patient first registers
Updated only when the patient asks to change it
Reviewed by reception, not the clinical team
Updated regularly, verbal check each visit
test.why: The written history is updated regularly and confirmed verbally at every appointment, with the answer recorded.

whyNot.0: A one-off history quickly goes out of date.
whyNot.1: Patients often don't realise a change matters, so the team must ask.
whyNot.2: The dentist reviews the history; the clinical team uses it to plan safe care.

explain.body: Use the history to prepare. Anxious patients and past fainters are treated lying flat. Diabetic patients should have eaten. Asthmatic patients bring their inhaler, angina patients their GTN spray. Allergies are flagged so the wrong material is never used.

test.q: A patient with insulin-treated diabetes says they haven't eaten today. Which emergency is now more likely?
options: Hypoglycaemia
Anaphylaxis
Angina attack
Asthma attack
test.why: Insulin without food lowers blood glucose, so hypoglycaemia becomes more likely.

whyNot.1: Anaphylaxis is triggered by an allergen, not a missed meal.
whyNot.2: Angina relates to heart blood supply, not missed meals.
whyNot.3: Asthma attacks are triggered by things like anxiety or allergens, not low blood glucose.

explain.body: Every team member is trained to their role. The GDC recommends 10 hours of medical emergencies CPD each five-year cycle, at least 2 hours a year. Scenario practice in the real setting, with a debrief, turns knowledge into fast teamwork.

test.q: After a scenario practice, what is the most useful next step?
options: File the certificate and move on
Repeat it only if the dentist failed
Debrief and fix the gaps found
Swap all of the roles permanently
test.why: The value of a scenario comes from the debrief: identifying what slowed the team down and fixing it.

whyNot.0: Without a debrief, the same mistakes happen in a real emergency.
whyNot.1: Learning applies to the whole team, not one person.
whyNot.3: Roles are allocated by the leader on the day; the point is to fix specific gaps.

explain.body: One leader takes charge and allocates roles: someone on airway and CPR, a caller for 999, a runner for the kit, oxygen and AED, a recorder for times and drugs, and reception to meet the ambulance and look after other patients.

test.q: During an emergency, who is best placed to meet the paramedics and guide them to the patient?
options: The person doing compressions
The receptionist
The team leader
The recorder
test.why: Reception can meet the crew at the door, clear the route and look after other patients while the clinical team stays with the patient.

whyNot.0: Compressions must not stop, so this person stays with the patient.
whyNot.2: The leader must stay and coordinate the response.
whyNot.3: The recorder needs to keep noting times and drugs given.
